name: Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov
desc: He has left the university for want of money and lives in a garret under the roof of a five-storied house, in debt to his landlady and avoiding her on the stairs. He is handsome, proud, and has been lying on his sofa for a month thinking about one thing.
why: Dostoevsky keeps us inside his head and never lets that be comfortable. I find I cannot hold him at a distance and cannot take his side either, which I think is the design.

name: Pulcheria Alexandrovna Raskolnikov
role: His mother, a widow in the provinces
desc: She lives on a pension of a hundred and twenty roubles and has borrowed against it to send her son money. We meet her first in a long letter.
why: The letter is one of the best things in the book: every reassurance in it tells him the opposite of what she means it to.

name: Avdotya Romanovna Raskolnikov
desc: She has been working as a governess in a household where the master pursued her, and has now accepted a proposal of marriage from a man she does not know well.
why: She has her brother’s pride and puts it to different use. The book keeps asking what the difference is.

name: Semyon Zaharovitch Marmeladov
role: A titular counsellor, dismissed; a drunkard
desc: He tells his whole story to a stranger in a tavern: the post he drank away, the wife he pities and fears, the daughter who supports them.
why: His speech is grotesque and it is also a real theology of the last judgement. Dostoevsky will not let you choose one.

name: Katerina Ivanovna Marmeladov
desc: Consumptive, well-born, with three small children from a first marriage, living in a passage room and scrubbing the floor at night out of pride.
why: She is cruel and she is wronged. Dostoevsky gives her more dignity the less she can afford it.

name: Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladov
role: “Sonia”. Marmeladov’s daughter by his first marriage
desc: Eighteen, timid, and since her stepmother’s reproach one evening the holder of a yellow ticket, which is to say a registered prostitute. Her earnings keep the family.
why: We hear about her long before we see her, and what we hear is her father’s account. It is worth noticing who gets to describe whom in this book.

name: Alyona Ivanovna
desc: A widow who lends on pledges at ruinous interest from a fourth-floor flat, behind a door she opens a crack at a time.
why: The first chapter makes us see her through his eyes, with every detail already an argument. Try seeing her without him.

name: Lizaveta Ivanovna
desc: Thirty-five, tall, meek, worked like a servant by Alyona, and known to everyone in the Hay Market, where she deals in second-hand clothes.
why: People in this novel talk about Lizaveta as if she were not quite there. The book notices.

name: Dmitri Prokofitch Razumihin
desc: Poor, loud, generous, always in the middle of some scheme for earning money by translation, and incapable of being offended for long.
why: He is the book’s proof that poverty and the ideas in the air do not have to end where they end for his friend.

name: Nastasya
role: The landlady’s cook and only servant
desc: A country woman who brings him tea and cabbage soup and tells him what she thinks of his lying about all day.
why: She asks him what work he does, he says “thinking”, and she laughs until she is ill. It is the soundest criticism he receives.

name: Zossimov
desc: Stout, well-dressed, pleased with himself, with a special interest in what he calls mental diseases.
why: He diagnoses everything and understands very little, which is the novel’s view of diagnosis.

name: Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin
role: A lawyer of forty-five with a little capital; engaged to Dounia
desc: He has let it be known that he prefers a wife who is poor, so that she will owe him everything. He is coming to Petersburg to open an office.
why: He has a theory too, about enlightened self-interest, and the book sets it beside the hero’s on purpose.

name: Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigaïlov
desc: The master of the house where Dounia was governess, whose attentions cost her the place. At the start we know him only by report.
why: Hold on to the name. Few characters in fiction are so thoroughly discussed before they open a door.

name: Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov
role: A clerk and a man of advanced ideas
desc: A lodger in the Marmeladovs’ building who talks of communes and the new principles.
why: Dostoevsky’s caricature of the Petersburg radical, drawn with more malice than fairness. He is allowed one fine moment all the same.

name: Porfiry Petrovitch
role: Examining magistrate; a relation of Razumihin’s
desc: About thirty-five, short, stout, with a round face and something womanish in it, forever laughing and screwing up his eyes.
why: The interviews with him are the best scenes of talk in the novel. Watch what he chooses not to ask.

name: Ilya Petrovitch
desc: A lieutenant with a reddish moustache standing straight out and a temper that goes off at a look.
why: Comic, and present at more turning points than a comic figure should be.

name: Nikodim Fomitch
desc: A handsome, good-natured officer who smooths over his lieutenant’s explosions.
why: Ordinary decency, in uniform, which this book treats as rare.

name: Zametov
role: Head clerk at the police office
desc: A fashionable young man of twenty-two with rings on his fingers and his hair parted and pomaded.
why: He is the one who nearly understands and is talked out of it.
